classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate probability arguments and explain why counting named outcomes requires equally likely outcomes.

content.prompt: Comment on the following arguments, whether they are correct or incorrect and why.

children.label: a
children.prompt: “When I buy a lottery ticket, there are only two outcomes, either I win or lose. So, the probability I win is 50%.”

answer.short: Incorrect. Winning and losing are not equally likely.
answer.worked: Having two possible outcomes does not make them equally likely. Winning a lottery is much less likely than losing, so the probability of winning is not $50\%$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: “When answering a multiple-choice test in which there are four possible answers to each question, the chance that Peter answers a question correctly is $\frac{1}{4}$.”

answer.short: Not necessarily correct. $\frac{1}{4}$ assumes Peter guesses randomly among four options with one correct answer.
answer.worked: If Peter guesses randomly, each of the four options is equally likely to be selected, so $P(\text{correct})=\frac{1}{4}$. Peter may know the answer or eliminate options, so the stated probability does not follow from the information given.

children.label: c
children.prompt: “A bag contains a number of red, white and black beads. If you choose one bead at random from the bag, the probability that it is black is $\frac{1}{3}$.”

answer.short: Not necessarily correct. The probability is $\frac{1}{3}$ only when one-third of all the beads are black.
answer.worked: $$P(\text{black})=\frac{\text{number of black beads}}{\text{total number of beads}}.$$ Three colours do not imply three equally likely outcomes. The probability is $\frac{1}{3}$ when one-third of the beads are black; the red and white counts need not be equal.
